notes: Eyskens IV (since June 1968) is a Christian democrat-Socialist coalition: ruling slot 1 holds Eyskens's Flemish CVP (the francophone PSC, autonomous since the 1968 Leuven crisis, is covered in its text); the real partner BSP-PSB sits in slot 3, while the template coalition slot 2 holds the opposition liberals PVV-PLP. Volksunie in slot 14 as in MD, FDF in slot 20 as the populist language-defence party. Maoist PC(ML)B in slot 19 (renamed PCMLB on 28 June 1970), Mandel's La Gauche network in 5, Thiriart's Jeune Europe in 6, pro-Soviet KPB hardliners in 7, Société Générale in 15 instead of MD's FEB. Only CVP, armed forces and royal house sprites reused.

0.name: Staatsveiligheid / Sûreté de l'État
0.text:
The State Security Service is Belgium's civilian intelligence and counter-espionage agency, attached to the Ministry of Justice. Since NATO moved its headquarters to Brussels and SHAPE to Casteau near Mons in 1967, the capital has become a hunting ground for Soviet and East European spies, and the service works closely with its American, British and French partners to counter them.

It keeps files on communists, Maoists, Trotskyists, Flemish and Walloon radicals, Palestinian activists and immigrant workers' organisations, and regards itself as a guardian of the Western order rather than of any party. It is secretive, conservative and answerable to few. Its leverage lies in surveillance, its archive of compromising information and its intimacy with Allied intelligence services.

1.name: Christelijke Volkspartij
1.text:
The Christian People's Party is the Flemish wing of Belgian Christian democracy, which since the Leuven crisis of 1968 has operated separately from its francophone sister, the Christian Social Party. Prime Minister Gaston Eyskens, an economist who first headed a government in 1949, has led a coalition with the Socialists since June 1968, while Robert Vandekerckhove chairs the party.

The CVP stands for Catholic schools and social organisations, a welfare state built with the Christian labour movement, European integration and loyalty to NATO. Its central task is a constitutional reform granting cultural autonomy to the communities and a new deal for the regions. Its strength lies in Catholic Flanders: the farmers' Boerenbond, the Christian unions, the middle-class federations and the parishes.

2.name: Partij voor Vrijheid en Vooruitgang
2.native_full: Partij voor Vrijheid en Vooruitgang / Parti de la liberté et du progrès
2.text:
The Party for Freedom and Progress was created in 1961 when Omer Vanaudenhove transformed the old anticlerical Liberal Party into a broad centre-right party open to Catholics. It won over a fifth of the vote in 1968 and is the main opposition to the Eyskens government. Its national president since 1969 is Pierre Descamps, but its Flemish, Brussels and Walloon wings are pulling apart.

The liberals stand for free enterprise, lower taxes, less state interference, a balanced budget and firm support for NATO and the Common Market. Unitarist by instinct, they resist a federal Belgium yet know reform is coming. Their base is business, the professions, the self-employed and the Brussels bourgeoisie, and their leverage lies in the votes needed for a two-thirds constitutional majority.

3.name: Belgische Socialistische Partij / Parti socialiste belge
3.native_full: Belgische Socialistische Partij / Parti socialiste belge
3.text:
The Belgian Socialist Party is the heir of the Belgian Workers' Party founded in 1885, and since June 1968 it has governed as the junior partner of the Christian democrats in Gaston Eyskens's coalition. Its president Léo Collard, whose education policy as minister in 1955 sparked the last school war, leads a party whose Walloon federations and Flemish wing, voiced by Jos Van Eynde, increasingly diverge.

The socialists defend the welfare state, public investment in declining Walloon industry, economic planning and secular state schools, while accepting NATO and European integration. Walloon members push for federalism and structural reforms. The party's power rests on the socialist unions, cooperatives and mutual societies, the industrial basins of Liège, Charleroi and the Borinage, and the docks of Antwerp and Ghent.

4.name: Kommunistische Partij van België / Parti communiste de Belgique
4.native_full: Kommunistische Partij van België / Parti communiste de Belgique
4.text:
The Communist Party of Belgium, founded in 1921, reached its peak after the liberation, when it sat in government, but it now polls about three per cent and holds a handful of seats. Its president since 1968, Marc Drumaux, has steered it towards a more independent line, and the party criticised the Soviet-led invasion of Czechoslovakia.

The party calls for nationalisation of energy and the holding companies, federalism with strong regions, Belgian withdrawal from NATO and peaceful coexistence. It seeks a progressive front with socialists and Christian workers. Its base lies in the coal and steel basins of Liège, Charleroi and the Borinage, among Antwerp dockers and veterans of the wartime Resistance, and its leverage in militant trade unionists.

5.name: La Gauche
5.text:
La Gauche is the weekly founded in 1956 by Ernest Mandel, the Brussels Marxist economist who leads the Fourth International, and the name of the Trotskyist network built around it and its Flemish twin Links. Expelled from the Belgian Socialist Party in 1964, its supporters have regrouped in small Walloon and Brussels workers' parties and are winning students radicalised in 1968.

The group calls for anti-capitalist structural reforms, workers' control, general strikes against austerity and a socialist United States of Europe. It condemns both the bureaucracy in Moscow and the socialists' coalition with the Christian democrats, and campaigns for Vietnam and against NATO. Its leverage lies in Mandel's international prestige and a few hundred militants in the unions and universities.

6.name: Jeune Europe
6.text:
Young Europe was founded in 1962 by Jean Thiriart, a Brussels optician and former collaborator, out of the agitation of Belgian settlers after Congo's independence. It spread across Western Europe, was later reorganised as the Communitarian European Party and published La Nation européenne. Thiriart, who met Zhou Enlai in 1966 and courted Arab regimes, withdrew from active politics in 1969, but his cadres and networks remain.

The movement rejects both American and Soviet domination and calls for a unitary, authoritarian European nation from Brest to Bucharest, allied with China and the Arab world against the superpowers. It hails the Palestinian fedayeen; one of its militants, Roger Coudroy, was killed fighting with Fatah in 1968. Its leverage is small: a few dozen militants and contacts across the national-revolutionary fringe.

7.name: Les Moscoutaires
7.text:
The Moscow Loyalists are the old guard of Belgian communism who never accepted the party's criticism of the Warsaw Pact intervention in Czechoslovakia in August 1968. Veterans of the wartime partisans and of the Cold War, strongest in the federations of the Liège and Hainaut coal basins, they look to the Soviet embassy and to the peace and friendship societies rather than to the party's new leadership.

They hold that loyalty to the Soviet Union is the test of every communist, and they distrust federalism, the opening to Christian workers and the leftist students alike. They want Belgium out of NATO, NATO out of Brussels and recognition of the German Democratic Republic. Their leverage is limited but real: Moscow's favour, East-West trade contacts and discipline among older militants.

8.name: Nadi Jabal Amil
8.text:
The Jabal Amil Club is a small association of Lebanese Shia traders from the hills of southern Lebanon who have settled in Antwerp, many of them after years in the diamond and import business of Congo, Sierra Leone and other African states. They meet in members' homes and shops for Muharram and Ramadan and send money to relatives around Tyre and Nabatieh.

The club follows Imam Musa al-Sadr, whose Supreme Islamic Shia Council began work in Beirut in 1969 to win a fairer share for Lebanon's Shia. It preaches a moderate, civic Shiism: education, charity, good relations with Christians and loyalty to the host country. Its leverage is modest, resting on family trade networks and the goodwill of Antwerp's diamond houses.

9.name: Anjoman-e Velayat
9.text:
The Guardianship Society is a small circle of devout Iranian students at the universities of Leuven, Liège and Ghent, sons of bazaar families sent abroad to study engineering and medicine. They meet for Friday prayers and mourning ceremonies and listen to tape recordings of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, exiled in Najaf since 1965, which pilgrims and merchants smuggle to Europe.

The circle believes that the Shah's rule is illegitimate and that the learned clergy must guide the community and the state. It denounces the Pahlavi dynasty's alliance with America and Israel, the secular reforms of the White Revolution and the moral corruption of the West. It has no weapons, few followers and no Belgian contacts; its leverage lies in its zeal and the networks it will take back to Iran.

10.name: Centre islamique et culturel de Belgique
10.english: Islamic and Cultural Centre of Belgium
10.native_full: Centre islamique et culturel de Belgique
10.text:
The Islamic and Cultural Centre of Belgium is the country's leading Muslim institution. King Baudouin has leased the Oriental Pavilion in Brussels' Cinquantenaire Park for 99 years to King Faisal of Saudi Arabia, and the Centre is converting it into the Great Mosque of Brussels with funds and staff provided through the Saudi-backed Muslim World League.

The Centre promotes an official, conservative Sunni Islam: prayers, Koranic instruction, imams for the Moroccan and Turkish workers recruited for the mines and factories since 1964, and talks with the authorities on recognising Islam as a state-supported religion. It keeps away from radical politics and reflects the views of its Saudi patrons. Its leverage lies in Gulf money and royal goodwill.

11.name: Hizb al-Tahrir
11.text:
Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Party of Liberation, was founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by the Islamic judge Taqi al-Din al-Nabhani and is banned throughout the Arab world for trying to win over army officers. In Brussels, Leuven and Liège a few Jordanian, Palestinian and Syrian students hold discreet study circles, watched by Belgian State Security and by informers of their own governments.

The party rejects nationalism, democracy, socialism and every Muslim government of the day, and works for a single caliphate ruling by Islamic law that would unite the believers and free Palestine. It avoids armed action, relying on propaganda and the patient conversion of officers and elites. In Belgium it has no organisation of weight; its influence ends at a few student rooms.

12.name: Milli Görüş
12.text:
National Outlook is the name Necmettin Erbakan's followers give to their Islamic revivalist doctrine. The engineer was elected an independent deputy for Konya in October 1969 after the Justice Party barred his candidacy. Among the Turkish miners and factory workers recruited for Limburg, Ghent and Brussels since 1964, a few devout men from Anatolian towns read his speeches and gather for prayers in improvised rooms.

The movement wants a Turkey guided by Islamic morality and independent of the West: heavy industry built by the nation, an end to usury, distance from the Common Market and solidarity with the Muslim world. In Belgium it seeks prayer halls, Koran courses for children and protection of Turkish identity. Its leverage is tiny but grows with every family that arrives.

13.name: Nationale Bank van België / Banque nationale de Belgique
13.native_full: Nationale Bank van België / Banque nationale de Belgique
13.text:
The National Bank of Belgium, founded in 1850, is the hub of a powerful economic technocracy that also includes the Planning Bureau and the senior officials of the Ministry of Finance. Its governor since 1957, Hubert Ansiaux, is a respected figure in European monetary diplomacy and sits on the committee of central bank governors of the Common Market.

The technocrats believe that a country divided by language and party must be steered by experts: a stable franc, balanced budgets, wage moderation, careful planning of investment and the conversion of the old Walloon coal and steel basins. They are wary of a federalism that would fragment economic policy and of the spending every community demands. Their leverage lies in credit, the currency and advice that no government can ignore.

14.name: Volksunie
14.text:
The People's Union was founded in 1954 to give Flemish nationalism a democratic voice after the discredit of wartime collaboration. Led since 1955 by the Brussels lawyer Frans Van der Elst, it won almost ten per cent of the vote and twenty seats in the Chamber in 1968, riding the wave of the campaign to make the University of Leuven wholly Flemish.

The VU demands a federal Belgium with broad self-government for Flanders, the defence of Flemish interests in Brussels and its periphery, and amnesty for those punished for collaboration. It is socially moderate, Catholic in temper and pragmatic in economics. Its base is young Flemish professionals, students, small business and nationalist families, and its leverage lies in the pressure it puts on the CVP.

15.name: Société générale de Belgique
15.text:
The Société Générale de Belgique, founded in 1822 by King William I, is the country's most powerful holding company and the symbol of Belgian high finance. Under its governor Max Nokin it controls a vast portfolio of banks, coal mines, steelworks, non-ferrous metals, electricity and engineering firms, and it was the main shareholder of the Union Minière du Haut-Katanga, whose Congolese mines Mobutu nationalised in 1967.

The Générale stands for private ownership, financial orthodoxy and the influence of the great holdings over national economic policy. It resists nationalisation, distrusts a federalism that would split a unified market and seeks new fields in Europe as Walloon heavy industry declines. Its leverage lies in its boardrooms, its bank and its intimacy with ministers of every party.

16.name: Vlaams Economisch Verbond
16.text:
The Flemish Economic Association was founded in 1926 by the Antwerp photographic industrialist Lieven Gevaert and other Flemish-minded entrepreneurs to build a Dutch-speaking business class in a country run by francophone finance. Based in Antwerp, it speaks for the family firms, exporters and new industries that are making Flanders the dynamic half of the Belgian economy.

The VEV stands for free enterprise, low taxation, flexible labour markets and lean government, and it wants economic decisions taken closer to the Flemish regions rather than in the boardrooms of the Brussels holdings. It welcomes foreign investment, the expansion of the port of Antwerp and the Common Market. Its leverage lies in the growing weight of Flemish industry and its ties with liberal and Christian democratic politicians.

17.name: Réserves naturelles et ornithologiques de Belgique
17.native_full: Réserves naturelles et ornithologiques de Belgique / Belgische Natuur- en Vogelreservaten
17.text:
Belgian Nature and Bird Reserves was founded in 1952 by naturalists and ornithologists to buy and manage threatened marshes, heaths and dunes, as industry, motorways and housing eat up the countryside. It works alongside the older Walloon society Ardenne et Gaume and is gaining members as the Council of Europe proclaims 1970 European Conservation Year.

The association stands for nature reserves, protection of birds and wetlands, limits on pollution and hunting and respect for the landscape in planning. It is non-party, bilingual and moderate, relying on scientists, teachers and amateur naturalists, and younger members are beginning to link nature with the wider pollution of air and water. Its leverage lies in its land, its expertise and growing public concern.

18.name: Algemeen Belgisch Vakverbond
18.native_full: Algemeen Belgisch Vakverbond / Fédération générale du travail de Belgique
18.text:
The General Federation of Belgian Labour is the socialist trade union confederation, rebuilt in 1945 and allied with the Belgian Socialist Party. Its general secretary since 1968, Georges Debunne, leads a movement still marked by André Renard, the Liège steelworkers' leader who inspired the great strike of the winter of 1960-1961 and the demand for Walloon self-government.

The union fights for structural reforms: control of the holding companies, public investment, economic planning and workers' control, together with higher wages and shorter hours. Its Walloon wing sees federalism as the way to save the declining industrial basins, while its Flemish wing is more moderate. Its leverage lies in its hundreds of thousands of members, its strike funds and its weight inside the Socialist Party.

19.name: Parti communiste (marxiste-léniniste) de Belgique
19.text:
The Communist Party (Marxist-Leninist) of Belgium was founded at La Louvière in November 1967 by militants who broke with Jacques Grippa, the pioneer of Belgian Maoism, accusing him of siding with Liu Shaoqi against the Cultural Revolution. With some 150 members in the Centre, the Borinage and Brussels, led by figures such as Fernand Lefebvre and the lawyer Michel Graindorge, it is the largest of the pro-Chinese splinters.

The party upholds Mao Zedong Thought, denounces Soviet social-imperialism and the revisionism of the official communists, and calls for a revolutionary workers' party to overthrow Belgian capitalism. It looks to China and Albania, has its own youth and student groups and courts miners and immigrant workers. Its leverage lies in militancy in a few pits and factories.

20.name: Front démocratique des francophones
20.text:
The Democratic Front of Francophones was founded in 1964 to resist the language laws that fixed a linguistic border and confined bilingual Brussels to its nineteen communes. It has since become the voice of the capital's French-speaking majority, winning seats in the 1965 and 1968 elections, and it works with the new Walloon Rally of François Perin.

The FDF demands that Brussels become a full region with its own institutions, that francophones in the Flemish suburbs keep their rights and that the language border be revised. It rails against Flemish encroachment, the old parties and the language rules imposed on Brussels civil servants. Its base is the Brussels middle classes, civil servants and shopkeepers, and its leverage lies in local elections and the constitutional reform.

21.name: Vlaamse Militanten Organisatie
21.text:
The Flemish Militant Organisation was founded around 1950 by Bob Maes as a disciplined stewarding corps for Flemish nationalist meetings and the annual IJzer pilgrimage at Diksmuide. Closely tied to the People's Union, its uniformed squads clash with francophone and leftist demonstrators, and many members come from families punished for collaboration after the war.

The VMO wants an ethnically defined Flanders, united in spirit with the Netherlands, an amnesty for wartime collaborators and the expulsion of French influence from Flemish soil. It despises parliamentary compromise, Belgian unitarism and communism, and cultivates discipline, marches and street confrontation, while a harder fringe drifts towards open neo-fascism. Its leverage lies in intimidation and its role as the strong arm of radical nationalism.

22.name: Belgische Krijgsmacht / Forces armées belges
22.text:
The Belgian Armed Forces are a conscript army built around the First Belgian Corps, stationed in West Germany as part of NATO's Northern Army Group, with an air force flying F-104 Starfighters and a small navy. Since 1967 Belgium has also hosted NATO headquarters in Brussels and SHAPE at Casteau, and its paracommandos proved their worth in the Stanleyville rescue in the Congo in 1964.

The officer corps is francophone-dominated, monarchist and devoted to the Atlantic Alliance. It worries about the language quarrels that now divide units and promotions, about short conscription and stagnant budgets. It stays out of politics, but its loyalty to the King and to a united Belgium makes it a silent guardian of the unitary state.

23.name: Koninklijk Huis van België / Maison royale de Belgique
23.native_full: Koninklijk Huis van België / Maison royale de Belgique
23.text:
The Belgian royal house, of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha descent, has reigned since 1831. King Baudouin, on the throne since his father Leopold III abdicated in 1951 after the Royal Question nearly split the country, is a devout, reserved monarch married to Queen Fabiola of Spain. His brother Prince Albert of Liège is heir, and Leopold lives in retirement at Argenteuil.

The Crown is constitutionally neutral but embodies the unity of a state threatened by its language conflict, and the King quietly encourages compromise on constitutional reform. It is Catholic, Atlanticist and close to the army and the old Congo interests. Its leverage lies in its role in forming governments, the loyalty of Belgians in all communities and moral authority in times of crisis.
